“If it works, don’t touch it.”

It sounds like sensible advice. Sometimes it is. But as a general engineering principle, it can be dangerous.

A system can work and still be fragile. It can pass its tests and still be difficult to change. It can serve users reliably today while quietly accumulating assumptions that make tomorrow’s changes slower, riskier, and more expensive.

Working is not the same as safe. Working is not the same as maintainable. And working today does not guarantee that a system will remain workable as its requirements and environment change.

That is the problem technical debt helps us describe.

The answer is not to refactor everything simply because it looks old or inelegant. It is to understand which compromises are creating real costs and address them before they constrain the product or the team.

What is technical debt?

The technical-debt metaphor is commonly credited to Ward Cunningham, who used it in 1992 to explain the consequences of taking a shortcut while developing software. Like financial debt, a shortcut can provide an immediate benefit while creating future costs. Those costs are the metaphorical interest: extra effort spent understanding code, adding workarounds, testing changes, and investigating regressions.

A practical definition is:

Technical debt is the future cost of additional work caused by software design, implementation, or technology decisions that make a system harder to change, operate, or extend.

Not every defect is technical debt, and not every imperfect line of code creates meaningful debt. A defect is something that is wrong; debt is a condition that makes future work more expensive or risky. They can overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

Debt can appear in architecture, code, testing, documentation, dependencies, and infrastructure. Unclear component boundaries, duplicated logic, unreliable tests, undocumented assumptions, and unsupported libraries can all make future work harder.

How a codebase starts to rot

A codebase rarely becomes difficult to maintain overnight. Its deterioration is usually gradual, as new features, deadlines, staff changes, and operational demands put pressure on the original design.

The following lifecycle is a mental model, not a formal or inevitable sequence. Teams can recover at any stage, and not every project follows the same path.

1. Rapid delivery

At the beginning, speed matters. Requirements are uncertain, the product is being validated, and the team may not yet know which parts of the system will survive.

A minimal implementation can be the right choice. The danger is when temporary decisions quietly become permanent foundations: a prototype becomes production code, a hard-coded value becomes a business rule, or a one-off workaround becomes a dependency.

The mindset is often: “It works. Ship it.” There is nothing inherently wrong with shipping a small solution. The problem is forgetting which parts were temporary and need to be revisited.

2. Patchwork growth

As features accumulate, developers extend existing modules, copy familiar patterns, and sometimes duplicate code because a shared abstraction would take longer to design.

Cleanup gets postponed: “We’ll clean it up later.” That can be a reasonable short-term trade-off. But when every cycle adds shortcuts and no time is reserved to review them, new code begins to depend on old assumptions.

3. Foundation cracks

Eventually, the cost of change becomes noticeable. A feature that once took an hour now takes days because developers must first understand existing behavior and identify side effects.

Bugs recur, onboarding takes longer, and confidence in the system drops. This is an important point to intervene: the system may still be manageable, but the warning signs are visible.

4. Fear of touching

Some files acquire a reputation: “Don’t touch that. It might break everything.”

This often reflects real problems: weak tests, hidden dependencies, unclear ownership, or behavior nobody fully understands. Developers work around the dangerous area instead of improving it, adding yet another layer of complexity.

5. Fragility crisis

Deployments become risky. Small changes trigger unexpected regressions, and the team spends more time stabilizing existing behavior than delivering improvements. The business may begin questioning whether further investment in the system is worthwhile.

6. Rewrite or abandonment

A rewrite or migration starts to look attractive. Sometimes replacement is justified, but it is not automatically cheaper or safer. A rewrite can discard years of business knowledge, reproduce old mistakes, and require the old and new systems to coexist.

The right question is not simply “Should we rewrite it?” but “Which constraints make the current system expensive, and is incremental remediation or replacement the lower-risk option?”

Recognizing the warning signs

No single metric can measure technical debt. Metrics are signals for investigation, not verdicts about code quality.

Code churn

Code churn measures how much code changes over time. Repeated changes to the same files can indicate unclear design, unstable requirements, defects, or rework.

High churn is not automatically bad: an actively developed feature will naturally change often. It becomes more useful when considered alongside defect rates, complexity, and the amount of rework required after changes.

Cognitive Complexity

Cognitive Complexity estimates how difficult code may be for a person to understand, particularly when control flow breaks away from a straightforward, linear reading path.

Deeply nested conditions, many branches, and several interacting responsibilities can make a function difficult to reason about. Guard clauses, clear naming, and smaller, focused functions can help. But splitting everything into tiny functions can make the overall flow harder to follow. The goal is comprehensibility, not a low metric score for its own sake.

I like to put the goal this way:

“If a lay person reads a piece of code, they should atleast be able to make some sense of it.”

This is an aspiration for readability, not a literal test that non-programmers must understand implementation details. Good code should communicate its intent clearly, even to someone who does not know the language or framework.

Duplication and risky code

Repeated code can mean that shared behavior has not been identified. It can also be intentional: two pieces of code may look similar but represent concepts that need to evolve independently. Duplication is a reason to investigate, not an instruction to abstract everything.

Another warning sign is code that developers are afraid to change. If a small modification can cause unpredictable regressions, the area may lack clear boundaries, adequate tests, or understandable behavior.

That leads to one of the most important principles in this discussion:

“If a piece of code is so fragile that it might break when touched, that’s exactly why we should touch it. Now. Not later.”

This does not mean making risky changes blindly or refactoring an entire system during a critical release. It means fragility should be treated as a reason to improve the code deliberately, not as a permanent excuse to avoid it. When possible, address the problem while already working in that area: understand the behavior, add tests, make a controlled change, and verify the result.

AI: accelerating delivery and debt

AI coding assistants can generate boilerplate, explain unfamiliar code, suggest tests, and help explore implementation options. They can also produce code that compiles while violating architectural conventions, mishandling edge cases, or introducing unnecessary dependencies.

The risk is not that AI-generated code is inherently poor. Human-written code can be just as flawed. The risk is accepting generated code without understanding or validating it.

Treat AI output like a contribution from a very fast developer who only knows what's obvious in the code and documentation. Review it against the project’s architecture, error-handling strategy, security requirements, general undocumented know-how, and tests. Ask why an approach was chosen, remove unnecessary code, and verify meaningful edge cases.

AI should expand a developer’s toolbox, not replace the judgment needed to choose the right tool. If a team optimizes only for the speed of code production, it may also accelerate the production of future maintenance work. AI, if not used wisely, can become technical debt as a service.

Managing and repaying technical debt

Debt becomes dangerous when it is invisible, unprioritized, or repeatedly deferred. Managing it requires more than asking developers to clean up after themselves.

  1. Make it visible. Record debt in the issue tracker. Describe the affected area and the cost it creates. “Refactor this service” is vague; explaining that one service mixes tax calculation and email delivery gives the team something concrete to assess.

  2. Prioritize by impact. Consider how often the area changes, how much time it adds to development, whether it contributes to defects or incidents, and whether upcoming work will make it more expensive to fix.

  3. Allocate time. Track debt alongside features and bugs. Teams can reserve capacity for remediation or schedule focused cleanup when justified. A dedicated debt sprint can help, but quality work should not be restricted to occasional cleanup weeks.

  4. Refactor safely. Improve code when working in the area, but keep the scope controlled. Understand existing behavior, add or improve tests, make one coherent change at a time, and verify the result.

  5. Use tools thoughtfully. Linters, static analysis, dependency scanners, duplication detectors, and platforms such as SonarQube can identify issues. Their findings are evidence to investigate, not automatic judgments about what must be fixed.

  6. Make it everyone's responsibility. Developers, testers, operations teams, and product managers all experience the cost of debt. The people who encounter the problem should help make it visible and prioritize it.

When is technical debt worth taking?

Not every shortcut is a mistake. A prototype may be the fastest way to validate an idea. A minimum viable feature may help test user behavior before investing in a general architecture. A deliberate implementation shortcut may be justified by a genuine time-sensitive business need.

The distinction is between a conscious trade-off and an accidental liability.

A good debt decision makes clear what is being deferred, why the trade-off is justified, what risks it introduces, and what event should trigger reconsideration. That trigger might be a new feature, a usage threshold, an unsupported dependency, a regulatory change, or the point at which the workaround begins slowing development.

Not every item needs an exact repayment date, but it should remain visible and be revisited. Debt is manageable when the team understands its cost and does not mistake a temporary shortcut for a permanent solution.

A historical reminder: the Year 2000 problem

The Year 2000 problem, or Y2K, illustrates how a technical constraint can create a large future remediation effort.

In earlier computing environments, memory and storage were expensive. Many systems represented years using two digits: 1999 might be stored as 99. Depending on how a program interpreted the value, 00 could be treated as 1900 rather than 2000, or cause date calculations and comparisons to behave incorrectly.

Not every system used two-digit years, and not every system was destined to fail at midnight on 1 January 2000. The risk depended on how dates were stored, compared, calculated, and exchanged across systems.

Organizations spent years identifying affected systems, changing code and data, testing integrations, and preparing contingencies. Estimates of worldwide remediation costs vary. An estimate of $ 300–600 billion was reported before the rollover. However, it is not a definitive audited total of final global spending.

Y2K was not simply a story about bad programmers. The original storage trade-off made sense in its context. The problem was that the assumption spread through systems and remained in place for years, while the cost of changing it grew.

The takeaway

Technical debt is not proof that a team has failed. Some debt is an unavoidable consequence of building software under uncertainty. The problem is allowing compromises to accumulate without understanding their cost.

A healthy codebase does not have to be perfect. It has to remain understandable, testable, and changeable as the product evolves.

Ship when shipping matters. Take shortcuts when they are justified. But make those decisions consciously, keep the resulting debt visible, and do not let fear of touching fragile code become the reason it stays fragile.

Thank you for reading. 🙏
